images.title: Pile of pebbles: 2 and 2
images.purpose: Show every game of two piles of 2 pebbles when you play second, and that after each of your moves the two piles are equal.
images.composition: Two rows of small states joined by arrows. The top row is the game where the friend takes 2 first; the bottom row is the game where the friend takes 1 first.
images.exact_structure: Plain white 16:9 canvas with two rows of game states joined by right pointing arrows. A STATE is two small piles side by side. A pile of 2 is two flat grey #6B7280 pebbles (rounded ovals, thin dark outline), one resting on the other. A pile of 1 is one such pebble. An empty pile is a dashed grey circle with no pebble. Under every state, its count is written. TOP ROW, 3 states: [2 and 2] then [0 and 2] then [0 and 0]. The left pile is the one that is emptied in the first move. Above the first arrow the text friend takes 2; above the second arrow the text you take 2. BOTTOM ROW, 5 states: [2 and 2] then [1 and 2] then [1 and 1] then [0 and 1] then [0 and 0]. Above the four arrows, in order: friend takes 1, you take 1, friend takes 1, you take 1. To the right of the last state of each row, the text you win in green #009E73. The states that come right after your moves, which are [0 and 0] in the top row, and [1 and 1] and the last [0 and 0] in the bottom row, each have a #CC79A7 ring around the whole state. BOTTOM LEFT corner: a small #CC79A7 ring sample with the text equal piles after your move. Nothing else is drawn.

images.takeaway: When you play second and answer each move so that the two piles are equal, you take the last pebble.
images.description: The two possible games from 2 pebbles and 2 pebbles, with the second player making the piles equal after every move.
images.context: The chapter's picture is two piles of pebbles. The numbers are the plan's own from the concept's worked example: piles of 2 and 2, you play second. The labels 2 and 2, 0 and 0, friend takes 1 and you take 1 appear more than once on the picture, on the rows where they belong.
images.teaching_notes: Trace each row with a finger. Ask: what is the same in the three ringed states? Then ask what to do if the friend takes 1 first. This is the small game that leads to the winning rule for 7 and 7.

image_decisions.why: Playing the small game on the page lets the student see what stays the same after every move of the second player.
